pages.title: Neurodiversity and mental health in adulthood: exploring the unique contributions of autism and ADHD to internalising problems
contributions: Applied a trait‑based dimensional approach to disentangle the unique contributions of autism and ADHD to internalising disorders in a large adult population (N≈5,000).
Demonstrated that ADHD traits are a stronger predictor of internalising problem diagnoses than autistic traits using multivariate logistic regression.

Replicated the population‑level findings in a clinical case‑control sub‑sample (n=292), confirming elevated odds of anxiety and depression for both autism and ADHD groups relative to neurotypical controls.
Provided nuanced evidence that an ADHD diagnosis is more closely linked to depression, whereas an autism diagnosis is more closely linked to anxiety.
Integrated openly accessible UK and US adult datasets with standardized autism and ADHD measures, enabling cross‑national comparison.
methods: Cross‑sectional observational design with a large general‑population sample and a clinical case‑control sub‑sample.
Trait‑based measurement of autistic and ADHD characteristics using established self‑report scales.
Binary logistic regression to estimate odds ratios for internalising problem diagnoses, controlling for age, sex, and education.
Correlation analysis and multicollinearity assessment (Variance Inflation Factor).
Group comparisons using chi‑square tests, ANOVA, and Bayes factors for the clinical sub‑sample.
datasets: General‑population dataset of 4,996 adults from the United Kingdom and United States (openly accessible, includes autism and ADHD trait measures).
Clinical case‑control sub‑sample of 292 adults (Autism n=73, ADHD n=73, Neurotypical n=146) drawn from the same broader cohort.
key_findings: ADHD traits significantly predict internalising problem diagnoses (OR = 1.04 per unit increase, p < 0.001) and explain more variance than autistic traits (OR = 1.02, p < 0.001).
Sex is a significant predictor (female sex associated with lower odds; OR = 0.62, p < 0.001).
In the clinical sub‑sample, both autistic and ADHD groups have higher odds of anxiety, depression, and combined internalising problems compared with neurotypical controls (all p < 0.05).
No significant difference between autism and ADHD groups in overall internalising odds, but ADHD is more strongly associated with depression while autism is more strongly associated with anxiety.
Model fit: χ²(4,990, N = 4,996) = 462.69, p < 0.001, McFadden R² = 0.07; VIF values ≤ 1.14 indicating low multicollinearity.
evaluated_on: Prediction of internalising disorder diagnoses (anxiety, depression, combined) from autism and ADHD trait scores in adult populations

pages.title: Causal Effects of Brain Structural Features on ADHD and ASD Risk: A Two-Sample Mendelian Randomization Study
contributions: Identified a positive causal association between increased surface area of the superior frontal gyrus and ADHD risk.
Discovered a protective causal effect of larger surface area in the lateral orbitofrontal gyrus against ASD.
Revealed white matter microstructure (mode of anisotropy) in the inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus and retro‑lenticular internal capsule as causal substrates for ADHD and ASD respectively.
Performed sex‑stratified MR analyses to explore potential sex‑specific genetic effects on neurodevelopmental disorders.
Implemented two‑step mediation MR to assess fMRI features as mediators between brain structure and disorder risk.
methods: Weighted median and weighted mode estimators
MR‑PRESSO global test for horizontal pleiotropy
Delta method for mediation effect estimation
datasets: GWAS summary statistics for ADHD from iPSYCH, PGC, and Swedish population register (≈20,183 cases, 35,191 controls)
GWAS summary statistics for ASD from the Autism Spectrum Disorder Working Group of the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium (14,709 cases, 1,874,637 controls)
ENIGMA white matter microstructure GWAS (mode of anisotropy)
Sex‑specific GWAS summary statistics (male‑only and female‑only cohorts) from combined PGC/iPSYCH datasets
key_findings: Increased surface area of the superior frontal gyrus is causally associated with higher ADHD risk (IVW P = 2.04E‑13; β = 4.28E‑02).
Larger surface area of the lateral orbitofrontal gyrus is protective for ASD (IVW P = 1.98E‑42; β = -0.098).
Higher mode of anisotropy in the inferior fronto‑occipital fasciculus is negatively associated with ADHD (IVW P = 3.36E‑70; β = -18.35).
Higher mode of anisotropy in the retro‑lenticular part of the internal capsule is negatively associated with ASD (IVW P = 1.37E‑04; β = 12.72).
No significant reverse causal effects were observed from ADHD or ASD to brain structural metrics.
limitations: The study acknowledges the inherent limitation of two‑sample MR, which relies on summary‑level data and cannot fully account for all sources of bias.
Potential horizontal pleiotropy was detected for some instrumental variables; although MR‑PRESSO and MR‑Egger were applied, residual pleiotropy may remain.
Analyses were restricted to cohorts of largely European ancestry, limiting generalizability to other ethnic groups.
Confounding by socioeconomic factors (e.g., education, coffee intake, smoking) could influence the instrumental variables, and additional sensitivity analyses were suggested.
future_work: Repeat MR analyses after excluding SNPs linked to potential confounders such as education and substance use.
Validate the identified causal relationships in independent, non‑European cohorts.
Extend sex‑specific MR to larger samples and explore underlying biological mechanisms.
Incorporate multivariable MR to jointly model multiple brain features and environmental factors.
Perform prospective longitudinal imaging studies to corroborate the mediation pathways.

pages.title: Brain-Charting Autism and Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Reveals Distinct and Overlapping Neurobiology
contributions: Constructed a lifespan brain reference chart using 75,241 typically developing individuals from 49 sites.
Introduced centile scoring of structural MRI metrics (GMV, WMV, sGMV, CT, CV, SA) for autism and ADHD cohorts.
Identified distinct global and regional neuroanatomical alterations for autism and ADHD, including overlapping patterns.
Demonstrated age‑by‑diagnosis and sex‑by‑diagnosis interaction effects on brain measures.
Provided an open‑access normative modeling pipeline and reference data for neurodevelopmental research.
methods: Generalized additive models of location, scale and shape (GAMLSS) to generate centile scores.
Processing of T1‑weighted structural MRI to extract total gray matter volume, subcortical GMV, white matter volume, cortical thickness, cortical volume, and surface area.
Statistical comparisons with false discovery rate (FDR) correction and spin‑test spatial permutation.
Sensitivity analyses using full sample and sex‑matched subsamples.
Exploratory subgroup analysis of co‑occurring autism and ADHD (n=203).
datasets: Combined T1‑weighted scans from 49 sites (7 cohorts) comprising 75,241 typically developing individuals.
Clinical autism cohort (size not explicitly stated, includes a subgroup of 203 with co‑occurring ADHD).
MRC AIMS Consortium and Lifespan Brain Chart Consortium data.
key_findings: Autistic individuals show significantly larger ventricular volume centiles and greater cortical thickness in the superior temporal gyrus, with increased cortical volume in the same region.
ADHD individuals exhibit significantly lower total cortical gray, white, and subcortical gray matter volume and surface area centiles, but higher mean cortical thickness centiles.
Age‑by‑diagnosis interaction: significant for autism in superior frontal gyrus cortical thickness centiles; for ADHD, cortical thickness centiles positively correlate with age.
Co‑occurring autism‑ADHD subgroup (n=203) displays unique neuroanatomical signatures (e.g., autistic males have greater subcortical GMV and ventricular volume).
Regional analyses reveal widespread decreases in cortical volume and surface area for ADHD, whereas autism shows limited regional effects (primarily superior temporal gyrus).
limitations: Data on secondary diagnoses were not available for all datasets and were heterogeneous across sites, potentially leading to missed cases.
Secondary diagnoses at some sites were confirmed by clinician consensus, while others relied on community‑based reports, reducing reliability.
The co‑occurring autism‑ADHD subgroup analysis was exploratory and limited to 203 individuals.
The ADHD sample had a narrower age range (5–21 years) compared with the autism sample.
Findings are based on cross‑sectional structural MRI; longitudinal trajectories and functional modalities were not examined.
future_work: Validate the centile framework prospectively and longitudinally across development.
Incorporate functional MRI and diffusion imaging to extend neurobiological profiling.
Expand the reference chart to include additional neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions.
Improve harmonization and completeness of secondary diagnosis information across sites.
Assess clinical utility of centile scores for individualized diagnosis and treatment planning.

pages.comparison_gap: The study did not compare its centile‑based normative modeling approach against other normative frameworks (e.g., Gaussian Process Regression) or traditional case‑control effect‑size analyses commonly used in autism and ADHD neuroimaging literature.
